newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mercedes seeks return to racing glory.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes seeks return to racing glory.

text.p: Four years after its return to Formula One motor racing, Mercedes-Benz is still trying to recapture its former glory as a leader in one of the world's most glamourous sports.

Mercedes, which left the sport in 1955 when one of its cars was involved in a horrifying crash at Le Mans, has notched only one Formula One victory since returning in 1994 with the Sauber team and then jumping in 1995 as engine supplier to McLaren.

More important, Mercedes needs more victories to win the attention of the German public, which displays allegiance to favourite son Michael Schumacher of Italy's Ferrari, such as it did briefly after winning the 1997 Australian Grand Prix.

The pressure to win will be particularly strong on McLaren Mercedes to earn a victory in Sunday's German Grand Prix on the Stuttgart-based carmaker's home turf and help revive interest in one of the greatest names in motor sports history.

The link between race wins and sales of family saloons may seem tenuous, but some industry experts say there is one, particularly at Mercedes, as it seeks younger buyers and tries to shrug off a sometimes stodgy image.

"The problem for Mercedes is that they have so far not had the winning streak. Unless Mercedes can put in a consistent performance, when they are in top three in every race, it could begin to be a problem for sales," said Krish Bhaskar of the Motor Industry Research Unit in Nice, France.

Along with heavy promotional efforts, which include Mercedes putting its famous three-point emblem on race cars, the carmaker is also hoping that ordinary buyers will believe that advances in race car design, brakes and engines eventually make their way down to regular cars.

The question is whether Mercedes' performance in Formula One, which had a cumulative television audience during the 1996 season of 41 billion viewers around the world in 100 countries, may soon have a negative impact in showrooms.

Mercedes sales have indeed risen in recent years since returning to Formula One racing, including a nearly six percent rise in global sales during the first six months of 1997. But that is clearly not due just to being involved in motor racing.

"Being in Formula One fits in quite well with our motor sports strategy but it is not be right to say that because we are successful on the track, then we are successful in the showroom," said Norbert Haug, the head of Mercedes-Benz motorsports.

But the carmaker is clearly hoping to reach younger potential buyers by reviving a history of Grand Prix victories not seen since Juan Manuel Fangio piloted the famous "Silver Arrow" cars to successive championships in the mid 1950s.
Briton David Coulthard's victory at the Australian Grand Prix gave Mercedes a chance to tout its future as well as rejuvenate the "Silver Arrow" name for its race cars.

But technical failures kept Coulthard and teammate Mikka Hakkinen of Finnland from winning at the British and Canadian Grands Prix even though the two drivers were among the top three contenders in the last five races.

Mercedes's Formula One performance has also overshadowed the dramatic success of Mercedes on the CART circuit in the United States, where it leads the manufacturing championship and sales were up about 25 percent in the first half of 1997.
The carmaker has also been successful in the German touring car competition since returning in 1988.
Marketing departments at major carmakers speak of a so-called "halo effect" from highly-publicised wins in big races that tend to bring buyers into showrooms.

Honda Motor Co of Japan is said to have been able to raise prices for its cars from one to five percent after dominating Formula One in the late 1980s. When Honda withdrew from the sport, they found their price position began to deteriorate.

Mercedes officials say Formula One victories will come with time. They also say the carmaker's ability to compete in such a brutally competitive sport, and also build what is considered the sport's most powerful engine with British partner Ilmore Engineering, is proof enough of Mercedes' capabilities.
Yet Mercedes officials concede there is no substitute for success at the Formula One level.
"Formula one is the top of the line," Hauk said.
